svg.aria-label: A simulated ripple tank used as a physical reservoir computer solving exclusive-or
svg.title: Pattern recognition in a bucket
svg.text: A tank of water computes something its own input cannot

g.text: one tank of water. Nothing inside it is ever adjusted.
Two switches. Answer YES when exactly one is on.
This is exclusive-or, and no straight line can carve it apart.
best a single straight line can do on the raw switches
— exactly chance. The information is there; the shape is wrong.
A problem with the wrong shape
Two switches, and the answer is YES when exactly one of them is on. A single linear rule cannot express that,
no matter how its coefficients are tuned. So we will not tune it — we will change the shape of the question instead.
Drive the switches into the water and watch.
Each switch turns a motor at the rim. The waves cross, reflect and interfere.
one linear fit — the only trained part
Three of the four stages have nothing to learn.
Let the physics do the work
Reservoir computing turns the usual arrangement inside out. The complicated part — the water — is left completely alone,
and the only thing fitted to the task is one straight-line readout at the very end.
Open the shutter for two wave periods.
The camera is a square-law sensor: it records brightness, which goes as the square of the
surface height — then saturates. That squaring is where the nonlinearity comes from.
If the water were linear, 1–1 would be exactly 0–1 plus 1–0.
Two motors running together do not simply add: their waves reinforce in some places and cancel in others, and the
camera's squaring turns that pattern into a genuinely new quantity. Without it, this trick provably cannot work.
Now fit one straight line — to the camera cells.
Same linear rule that failed on the switches, same XOR target. Only the input has changed.
each dot is one run the readout had never seen — 40 in all
correct on held-out runs, up from 50%
388 cells are read, but only about 30 carry independent information
unchanged across four orders of magnitude of regularisation
The water changed the shape of the question
Nothing was taught to the tank. Its ripples simply spread two bits across hundreds of vantage points, and in that
spread the answer became something a straight line could reach. This is what a computational fiber is being asked to do.

svg.text: Damped 2D wave equation on a 120×120 grid (γ·dt=0.0015, c=0.45), read by a saturating square-law camera on a 22×22 grid. The water frames above are 36 consecutive steps of that simulation.
One ridge-regression readout, trained on 40 runs and scored on 40 independent runs. After Fernando & Sojakka (2003), “Pattern recognition in a bucket”.
